sections.text:
A man is seventy-five years old, and God tells him to leave. “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house,” and go to the land that God will show him. He is to go to a land that he has not yet been shown. His name is Abram, and he goes. That moment, in chapter 12, is where the whole book turns.

Before it, Genesis is the book of beginnings. Chapters 1 to 11 tell of creation, the first sin, the flood and the tower of Babel. From chapter 12 it narrows to one family: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac, Jacob and his twelve sons, and Joseph in Egypt.

The thread through it all is God’s promise to Abraham of land, descendants and blessing. Its widest reach is the promise that “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” The book ends with the family safe in Egypt, and the promise still open.

Genesis is the first of the five books of the Law, which Jewish and Christian tradition link with Moses. Many scholars think these books reached their final form over a long period, drawing on older material. The book itself names no author. Its stories are set in Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt, in a world of herders, city states and great empires.

Christians read Genesis as the foundation for the rest of Scripture: God as creator, people made in his image, the entrance of sin, and the promise that the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ.

They differ on how chapters 1 to 11 relate to history and science. Some read them as a plain historical account. Some read them as history told in a highly shaped and symbolic way. And some read them chiefly as teaching about God and humanity.

Genesis 1 tells of God making the world in six days. God speaks, and what he names comes to be: light, sky, land and seas, plants, sun, moon and stars, sea creatures and birds, land animals and finally human beings. A refrain runs through the chapter: “God saw that it was good”, and at the end, “it was very good”.

Many readers notice a pattern in the days. On the first three, God forms spaces: light and darkness, sky and sea, dry land. On the next three, he fills them: lights for day and night, birds and fish, animals and people. Human beings are made “in his own image” and are told to fill the earth and have dominion over the other living things (verses 26 to 28).

Genesis is the first of the five books of the Law, which Jewish and Christian tradition link with Moses. Many scholars think these books reached their final form over a long period, drawing on older material. Christians hold different views on that, and the chapter itself names no author.

Other peoples of the ancient Near East also told how the world began, often as a struggle between gods. Read against that setting, Genesis 1 stands out: one God makes everything by speaking, without a fight, and the sun, moon and stars are things he made.

Christians agree that this chapter presents God as the maker of everything and people as made in his image. They differ on how the six days relate to the age and history of the universe.

- Some read the days as six ordinary days.
- Some read each day as a long age.
- Some read the week as a literary framework that teaches who made the world and why, without giving a timetable.

Each of these views is held by Christians who take Scripture seriously. The words “Let’s make man in our image” (verse 26) are also discussed: some see a first hint of the Trinity, others a royal way of speaking, or God addressing his heavenly court.

sections.text:
The work of creation is finished, and God rests on the seventh day and makes it holy. Then the story slows down and draws close. There is no rain yet and no one to farm the ground, only a mist rising from the earth. The LORD God forms a man from the dust and breathes into his nostrils the breath of life. He plants a garden in Eden, with a river that parts into four, and he puts the man there to cultivate it and keep it. He may eat from every tree but one, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Then comes the first thing in the whole story that is not good: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” The man names the animals, but none is a companion for him. God causes a deep sleep to fall on him and builds a woman. The man cries out, “bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.” The chapter ends with the two of them together, naked, and “they were not ashamed.”

Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 each tell of creation, with a different focus: the first looks at the whole cosmos, this one at the garden and the first man and woman. Many scholars see two accounts brought together; many Christians read them as one story told two ways. Tradition links Genesis to Moses. Christians differ on how literally to read the details, and on what the man’s creation first and the woman’s from his side say about men and women.

A quiet voice interrupts the garden. The serpent asks the woman, “Has God really said” that they may not eat from any tree? She answers with what God said, and the serpent tells her she will not die but will be like God. She sees that the fruit is good for food and a delight to the eyes, and she takes it and gives some to her husband, who is with her. Their eyes are opened. They know they are naked, sew fig leaves, and hide when they hear the LORD God walking in the garden.

God calls, “Where are you?” The man blames the woman, the woman blames the serpent, and God speaks to each. The serpent is cursed. The woman will have pain in childbirth. The ground is cursed for the man’s sake, and he will return to dust. Yet God also promises that the woman’s offspring will bruise the serpent’s head. He makes clothes of animal skins for them, then sends them out of Eden, with cherubim and a flaming sword guarding the way to the tree of life.

This is the chapter behind the Christian teaching on the fall. Christians differ on the details, such as how far sin and death passed to all people. The words in verse 16 about the woman’s desire and her husband’s rule describe what comes after the break; Christians differ on whether they are a description or a command, and they have sometimes been misused to excuse domination. Many Christians read verse 15 as the first hint of a rescue (see Romans 16:20).

Eve gives birth to a son and says she has gotten a man with the LORD’s help. Then a second son is born. Cain farms, and Abel keeps sheep. Each brings an offering, and the LORD respects Abel’s but not Cain’s. Cain is very angry, and his face falls. God speaks to him gently: if he does well, will he not be lifted up? And if not, “sin crouches at the door.”

Cain says to his brother, Let’s go into the field, and there he kills him. When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” God says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.” Cain becomes a wanderer, afraid for his life, and God marks him so that no one will kill him. The chapter follows Cain’s line, with a city and craftsmen and a boastful song of Lamech, and ends with Seth, whose son Enosh is born in a time when people began to call on the LORD’s name.

The first death in the Bible is a murder between brothers. The text does not say why the offering was not respected; the New Testament links it to the heart of the giver (see Hebrews 11:4 and 1 John 3:12). Notice that God speaks to Cain before and after, and protects him even after the crime. Lamech’s song takes the sevenfold protection and turns it into boasting of seventy-seven times. The chapter moves from violence to the beginning of worship.

The chapter is a list, and it reads like a slow drumbeat. It begins with Adam, made in God’s likeness, and he fathers Seth in his own likeness. Then names follow, each with a number of years and, again and again, the same sad word: “then he died.” Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Methuselah, Lamech, each living many centuries and having other sons and daughters.

One name breaks the pattern. Of Enoch the text says, “Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.” He lived three hundred sixty-five years, far fewer than the others, and no death is recorded. Near the end, Lamech names his son Noah and says, “This one will comfort us in our work”. The chapter ends with Noah at five hundred years old, the father of three sons.

Genealogies like this one carry the story from Adam to Noah and show that the blessing of Genesis 1 continues even in a world under the curse. Readers differ on the very long lifespans: some read them literally, others as literary or symbolic. Enoch is remembered again in the New Testament (see Hebrews 11:5 and Jude 14). Lamech’s hope for Noah looks back to the cursed ground of Genesis 3 and forward to the flood.

Something has gone wrong with the world. When people multiplied, the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful and took wives for themselves, and the Nephilim were on the earth. The LORD limited human days to one hundred twenty years. He saw that the wickedness of man was great and that every thought of the heart was only evil, and “it grieved him in his heart.” He resolved to blot out man and the animals.

“But Noah found favor in the LORD’s eyes.” He was a righteous man, blameless in his time, and he “walked with God.” The earth was corrupt and full of violence, so God told Noah to build a ship, giving him its length, width and height, with a roof and a door in its side. God would bring a flood, but he would also keep a covenant with Noah, his wife, his sons and their wives. Noah would bring two of every kind of living thing into the ship. Noah did all that God commanded him.

The meaning of the sons of God in verses 1 to 4 is old and disputed. Some Jewish and Christian readers take them to be heavenly beings, others the descendants of Seth, others powerful rulers. The point the text itself makes is that violence had spread. The chapter shows both God’s grief and his choice of one family to carry a future. The New Testament holds up Noah’s faith (see Hebrews 11:7).

The LORD tells Noah, “Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation.” He is to take seven pairs of every clean animal and birds, and two of the unclean. In seven days the rain will fall for forty days and forty nights. Noah does everything the LORD commands. He is six hundred years old when the flood comes.

On the seventeenth day of the second month, “the fountains of the great deep burst open,” and the windows of the sky open. Noah, his wife, his sons and their wives go into the ship with the animals, pair by pair, male and female. Then the LORD shuts him in. The waters rise and lift the ship above the earth until even the high mountains are covered. Everything that breathed on dry land dies, and only Noah and those with him in the ship are left. The waters flood the earth for one hundred fifty days.

The chapter reads like a record, with dates, numbers and repeated phrases, and it shows the world undone: the waters above and below, divided in Genesis 1, come together again. Stories of a great flood are told by other ancient peoples too, and many scholars compare them. Christians differ on whether the flood was worldwide or regional. The text itself says that God shut the door, and that those inside were kept alive. It does not hide the loss of life.

“God remembered Noah” and every living thing with him in the ship. He sends a wind over the earth, the springs of the deep and the windows of the sky are closed, and the waters begin to go down. On the seventeenth day of the seventh month the ship comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven, and then a dove, which finds nowhere to rest and returns. A week later he sends her again, and this time she comes back in the evening with “a freshly plucked olive leaf.” After another week she does not return.

At last the ground is dry, and God tells Noah to come out. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. The LORD smells the pleasing aroma and says in his heart that he will never again curse the ground or strike every living thing, although “the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” While the earth remains, seed time and harvest will not cease.

The turning point is in the first verse: God remembers. In the Bible, to remember is to act on a promise. The chapter is full of small details of waiting, with seven days, then seven more, and each time a bird. The LORD’s promise comes in the same breath as his honest view of human hearts, so mercy rests on grace and not on human goodness. The altar and offerings recall worship in Genesis 4, and the promise leads to the covenant of the next chapter.

God blesses Noah and his sons with the old words, “Be fruitful, multiply”. The animals will fear them, and every moving thing may be food, but not flesh with its blood in it. God will require a reckoning for human life, “for God made man in his own image.” Then God makes a covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature: never again will a flood destroy the earth. As a sign he says, “I set my rainbow in the cloud,” and when he sees it he will remember.

The last part is darker. Noah plants a vineyard, drinks the wine and becomes drunk, uncovered in his tent. Ham sees his father and tells his brothers, while Shem and Japheth walk in backwards with a garment to cover him. When Noah wakes he says, “Canaan is cursed”, and blesses Shem and Japheth. Noah lives three hundred fifty years after the flood and dies at nine hundred fifty.

The covenant is made with all living creatures, and its sign is a bow hung in the sky. The last scene is hard and unclear. The curse falls on Canaan, Ham’s son, and not on Ham, and the text does not say why. It was later misused in modern history to defend the enslavement of people of African descent; the text does not support that, and it names no such people. The chapter also holds the first call for justice in human life, in verses 5 and 6.

After the flood, the chapter lists the families that spread over the earth. The sons of Japheth are named first, then the sons of Ham, and then the sons of Shem. Under each come their children and the lands where they settled, each “after his language, after their families, in their nations.” Among the names, one stands out: Cush became the father of Nimrod, “a mighty hunter before the LORD”, whose kingdom began in Babel and spread to Nineveh. Canaan’s family is traced with its borders from Sidon to Gaza and toward Sodom and Gomorrah. In Eber’s family one son is named Peleg, “for in his days the earth was divided.”

The chapter ends with a summary: these are the families of the sons of Noah, and the nations divided from them on the earth after the flood.

This list is often called the table of nations. It places all peoples in one family and ends by saying that nations spread from the three sons of Noah. Many names are places or peoples in the ancient Near East, and scholars still discuss how to identify them. The Bible’s later story of Israel takes place among these neighbors. The chapter sets the stage for Genesis 11, where the mention of Babel returns. The New Testament speaks of one human family (see Acts 17:26).

The whole earth speaks one language. Traveling east, people settle in a plain in Shinar and learn to make bricks, with tar for mortar. They say, “let’s make a name for ourselves,” and build a city and a tower whose top reaches the sky, so that they will not be scattered. But the LORD comes down to see the city and the tower. He sees that they are one people with one language, and he confuses their speech so that they no longer understand each other. They stop building, and the LORD scatters them. The city is called Babel.

Then the chapter slows into another genealogy, from Shem down to Terah. It ends with the story of one family. Terah fathers Abram, Nahor and Haran. Haran dies in Ur of the Chaldees, and Abram’s wife Sarai “was barren.” Terah takes Abram, Sarai and Lot toward Canaan, but they stop in Haran, and there Terah dies.

The tower story explains why people speak different languages, and many scholars link the name Babel to Babylon. Readers have understood the sin in different ways: as pride, as a refusal to spread over the earth as God had told them, or as a wish for security apart from God. The reversal is often seen at Pentecost (see Acts 2). The final verses prepare for Abram’s call: after the nations are scattered, God chooses one family, and it begins with a childless couple.

Abram is seventy-five, and God’s word reaches him: “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.” With the command comes a promise of a great nation, a great name and a blessing for others. Abram leaves with Sarai, Lot and all their people. In Canaan, at Shechem, the LORD appears to him and says he will give this land to his offspring, and Abram builds an altar. He builds another near Bethel and calls on the LORD’s name.

Then famine drives him down to Egypt, and fear overtakes him. He asks Sarai, “Please say that you are my sister”. She is taken into Pharaoh’s house, and Abram gains sheep, cattle and servants because of her. The LORD afflicts Pharaoh’s house with plagues. Pharaoh calls Abram to him, asks what he has done, and sends him away with his wife and all that he had.

This is where the story of Israel begins. God’s promise has three parts: a land, a people and a blessing that reaches “All the families of the earth” (verse 3). The New Testament returns to it often (see Galatians 3 and Hebrews 11). The Egypt episode shows a man of faith acting out of fear, and the text does not praise his lie. Pharaoh, a stranger, is the one who tells Abram what he has done wrong. Readers differ on how to judge Abram here.

Abram comes up out of Egypt, very rich in livestock, silver and gold, and returns to the altar he built between Bethel and Ai. But Lot is rich too, and the land cannot hold both their herds. Their herdsmen quarrel. Abram, the elder, speaks first: “let there be no strife between you and me,” for we are relatives. He lets Lot choose. Lot looks over the plain of the Jordan, well watered “like the garden of the LORD,” and takes it, moving his tent as far as Sodom. The narrator adds that the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked.

After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to lift up his eyes in every direction, for all the land he sees will be given to him and his offspring forever. They will be as many “as the dust of the earth”. Abram moves to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar to the LORD.

Abram, who has the promise, gives way, and Lot, who sees the best land, moves toward trouble. The text does not say that Lot was wrong to choose, but it points ahead to Sodom (see Genesis 19). God speaks to Abram only after Lot leaves. The land promise appears here with its widest bounds, and Christians and Jews have read it in different ways. The altars at the start and end of the chapter mark the places where Abram worships.

Four kings from the east march against five kings of the cities near the Salt Sea, and the five lose. The victors carry off the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and with them Lot, Abram’s nephew. A survivor brings word to Abram, who gathers his three hundred eighteen trained men, pursues the raiders by night and brings back the goods, Lot, and the people.

On his return two kings come out to meet him. The first is Melchizedek king of Salem, “priest of God Most High”, who brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth.” Abram gives him a tenth of everything. The second is the king of Sodom, who tells Abram to keep the goods and return the people. Abram refuses to take even “a thread nor a sandal strap”, so that no one can say he made Abram rich.

Melchizedek appears out of nowhere and vanishes again. He is remembered in Psalm 110 and discussed in Hebrews 7, where Christians see him as a figure who points to Christ. Many readers take Salem to be Jerusalem. The story shows Abram acting as a rescuer and refusing a reward from a king who dishonors God, though he lets his allies take their share. Christians and Jews read the tithe and the blessing as signs of how Abram stood before God.

Abram is afraid, and he is childless. In a vision the LORD tells him not to be afraid, and Abram answers with the ache beneath everything: he has no child, and a man of his household will inherit. The LORD says no. A son from his own body will. Then he takes Abram outside. “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Abram believed, and the LORD “credited it to him for righteousness.”

Yet Abram asks how he will know he will inherit the land. What follows is strange and solemn. Animals are cut in two and laid in rows, birds of prey come down, and at sunset a deep sleep and great darkness fall on him. He hears of four hundred years of hardship for his offspring, and then a smoking furnace and a flaming torch pass between the pieces. That day the LORD makes a covenant and names the land.

Abram has left Ur and his home behind, and this is one of the places where the LORD speaks to him most plainly about the promise of a son and a land. Many scholars see the cut animals as an ancient way of sealing a covenant. The New Testament returns to the line about believing: see Romans 4 and Galatians 3. The four hundred years of hardship look ahead to the story that begins in Exodus.

Sarai has no child, and in her house lives a servant, an Egyptian named Hagar. Sarai gives her to Abram as a wife, hoping to obtain children through her. Hagar conceives, and the household breaks apart. Sarai blames Abram, Abram tells her to do as she sees fit with Hagar, and Sarai deals harshly with her. Hagar runs into the wilderness.

By a spring on the way to Shur the LORD’s angel finds her and asks where she has come from and where she is going. He tells her to return, promises offspring too many to count, and says she will bear a son and call him Ishmael, because the LORD has heard her affliction. Hagar names the one who spoke to her: “You are a God who sees,” she says. The well is called Beer Lahai Roi. Then Hagar bears her son, and Abram is eighty-six.

The chapter is hard reading. A servant is given away, used and then mistreated, and the text tells it without softening it. Hagar is the first person in Genesis to give God a name. Her story returns in Genesis 21, and Paul uses it in Galatians 4. Muslims also honor Hagar and Ishmael, and Jews and Christians read the chapter with them in mind.

Abram is ninety-nine years old when the LORD appears to him again. “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be blameless.” Abram falls on his face. God speaks of a covenant that will last, of many nations and kings, and of the land. Abram becomes Abraham, and Sarai becomes Sarah, who will be a mother of nations.

God also gives a sign: every male in Abraham’s house, a baby of eight days or a servant bought with money, is to be circumcised. Then Abraham laughs, in his heart, at the thought of a child at one hundred, and he asks that Ishmael might live before God. God answers that Sarah will bear Isaac within a year, and that Ishmael is heard and blessed, with twelve princes to come from him. That very day Abraham circumcises Ishmael and every male in the house.

The promise made in Genesis 12 and 15 is now given a sign on the body and new names. Jewish practice still circumcises sons on the eighth day. Christians have read the chapter in different ways, and the New Testament takes up the question of the sign in places such as Acts 15 and Romans 4. The laughter in this chapter prepares for the name Isaac in the next.

It is the heat of the day, and Abraham sits at the door of his tent. He looks up and sees three men standing near. He runs to meet them, bows to the ground and begs them to stay. Water for their feet, bread, a calf, butter and milk: he hurries, and Sarah hurries with him.

Then comes the question, “Where is Sarah, your wife?” Next year, one says, she will have a son. Sarah, listening behind the tent door, laughs to herself. “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” Sarah denies the laugh because she is afraid, and the answer is, No, you did laugh.

When the men look toward Sodom, the LORD says he will not hide what he is about to do. Abraham steps forward and bargains for the city, from fifty righteous people down to ten: “Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

The text moves between the three men and the LORD, so readers have taken the visitors in more than one way. Some Christian traditions see a hint of the Trinity here. Others read the LORD with two angels, as the next chapter suggests. The New Testament praises this kind of hospitality in Hebrews 13. Abraham’s prayer for Sodom is among the earliest prayers of intercession in the Bible.

Evening falls, and two angels come to Sodom. Lot rises from the gate, bows and takes them into his house. Before bedtime the men of the city, young and old, surround the house and demand that the visitors be brought out. Lot steps outside and shuts the door behind him. He pleads with them, and he offers his own daughters instead. The crowd presses on him, and the visitors pull him inside and strike the men at the door with blindness.

The visitors warn Lot that the city will be destroyed. At dawn the angels seize the hands of Lot, his wife and his daughters and lead them out with a warning: “Don’t look behind you,” and run. Sulfur and fire fall from the sky, and Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. The chapter ends in a cave in the hills, with Lot’s daughters, wine and the births of Moab and Ammon.

This is one of the hardest chapters in Genesis. Readers differ on how to understand the sin of Sodom: the mob here threatens violence against guests, and other passages speak of it, such as Ezekiel 16 and Luke 17. Lot’s offer of his daughters and the cave scene are told without a verdict from the narrator, and readers have long found them disturbing. Moab and Ammon become neighbors of Israel; Ruth, a Moabite, appears in Ruth 1.

Abraham has traveled south and now lives as a stranger in Gerar. He tells people that Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech sends and takes her. That night God comes to Abimelech in a dream: he is a dead man, because the woman is a man’s wife. Abimelech protests. He has not touched her, and he acted in the integrity of his heart. God says he knows it, that he himself kept Abimelech from sin, and that Abraham is a prophet who will pray for him.

Early in the morning Abimelech tells his servants, and they are scared. He calls Abraham in: “You have done deeds to me that ought not to be done!” Abraham explains his fear that there was no fear of God in this place, and that Sarah is also his father’s daughter. Abimelech gives Abraham sheep, cattle and servants, restores Sarah, and tells her she is vindicated. Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech’s house.

Two other stories in Genesis are close to this one: Genesis 12, where Abraham does the same in Egypt, and Genesis 26, where Isaac does it in Gerar. Many scholars think they are related traditions, and others take them as separate events. Here, strikingly, a foreign king shows integrity while Abraham is shown afraid. Abraham is called a prophet in verse 7, the first time the Bible uses that word.

At last the LORD does for Sarah what he had said. She conceives and bears Abraham a son in his old age, and Abraham names him Isaac and circumcises him at eight days. Sarah says, “God has made me laugh.”

The joy cracks at the feast for Isaac’s weaning. Sarah sees Ishmael mocking and demands that Abraham cast out Hagar and her son. It is very grievous to Abraham. God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael too will become a nation. Abraham sends Hagar away with bread and a container of water. In the wilderness the water runs out, and she puts the boy under a shrub and sits far off, weeping. The angel of God calls from the sky: “God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.” God opens her eyes to a well.

The chapter closes with Abimelech, a dispute over a well and a covenant at Beersheba.

The name Isaac is usually linked to laughter, and the chapter plays on it. The expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael troubles many readers, and the text itself has God speak of their future. Paul reads this story in Galatians 4. Jews, Christians and Muslims all honor Ishmael and Hagar in their own ways. Beersheba becomes a place Abraham and Isaac return to.

The chapter begins with a sentence that stops the breath: God tested Abraham. He is to take his son, his only son, Isaac, whom he loves, and offer him as a burnt offering in Moriah. Abraham says, “Here I am,” and rises early. For three days he walks, then leaves the young men behind, saying he and the boy will worship and come back. Isaac carries the wood. Abraham carries the fire and the knife.

Isaac asks where the lamb is. Abraham answers, “God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” At the altar Abraham binds Isaac and takes the knife. The LORD’s angel calls his name twice and says, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him.” A ram is caught in a thicket, and Abraham offers it instead. He names the place The LORD Will Provide, and the LORD repeats his promise of blessing for all nations.

Jewish tradition calls this story the binding of Isaac. Christians have often seen in it a foreshadowing of Christ, while others read it first as a test of Abraham’s trust; the New Testament mentions it in Hebrews 11 and James 2. The Law elsewhere forbids child sacrifice, as in Deuteronomy 12, and in the story the child is spared. Tradition links Moriah with Jerusalem; see 2 Chronicles 3.

Sarah dies at one hundred twenty-seven, in Kiriath Arba, also called Hebron. Abraham comes to mourn for her and weep. Then he rises from his dead and does what must be done. He goes to the people of the land and says, “I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you.” He asks for a burying-place.

The Hittites answer with respect: he is a prince of God among them, and he may bury his dead in the best of their tombs. Abraham bows. He asks for one thing, the cave of Machpelah at the end of Ephron’s field, and he asks to pay the full price. Ephron, sitting among his people at the city gate, offers to give it. Abraham insists. Four hundred shekels of silver are weighed out before all who went in at the gate. Abraham buries Sarah in the cave.

Abraham has been promised the whole land, yet the first piece he owns is a grave. The scene reads like an open-air contract in the city gate. Later Genesis says that Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob were buried in this cave; see Genesis 25, 35 and 49. Tradition links Machpelah with a site in Hebron that Jews and Muslims both revere.

Abraham is old, and he has one task left. He makes his oldest servant swear that Isaac will not marry a Canaanite, and sends him to Abraham’s own relatives. At evening he stops by the well outside the city of Nahor and prays for a sign: the young woman who offers him a drink, and also his camels, will be the one.

Before he finishes speaking, Rebekah comes with her pitcher on her shoulder. She gives him water, and then draws for all the camels. The servant asks, “Whose daughter are you?” She is Bethuel’s. At her brother Laban’s house he tells his message, and the family says it comes from the LORD. In the morning they ask her, “Will you go with this man?” She answers, “I will go.”

Isaac is walking in the field at evening when the camels come. Rebekah veils herself. Isaac brings her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and “He loved her.” He is comforted.

This is the longest chapter in Genesis, and it is told twice over, first as the events and then in the servant’s own account. It links back to the end of Genesis 22, where Rebekah’s family is named. In the world of the text marriages were arranged by families, yet Rebekah is asked for her own answer. The servant does not name himself; his task is to keep Isaac in the land of promise.

Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, and has more sons. Yet he gives all that he has to Isaac. At one hundred seventy-five, a good old age, he dies, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him in the cave beside Sarah. Ishmael’s sons are listed, twelve princes, and then Ishmael dies too.

Then the focus narrows to Isaac and Rebekah. She is barren, and Isaac entreats the LORD. She conceives, and the children struggle within her until she asks, “If it is like this, why do I live?” The LORD says, “The elder will serve the younger.”

Two boys are born. Esau comes out red, and Jacob comes with his hand on Esau’s heel. Esau grows to be a hunter, Jacob a quiet man who lives in tents, and each parent has a favorite. One day Esau comes in from the field, famished, and Jacob is boiling stew. He asks for the birthright first. Esau swears. “So Esau despised his birthright.”

The phrase this is the history of the generations marks new sections of Genesis, and many scholars see it as the book’s structure. Here the story turns from Abraham to Isaac’s sons. Christians differ on how Paul’s use of the oracle in Romans 9 applies God’s choice of Jacob; the prophet Malachi also returns to it. Esau is linked with Edom, as chapter 36 says.

A famine strikes the land, and Isaac goes to Gerar. The LORD appears and tells him not to go down to Egypt, but to live in the land, and repeats to him the promise given to Abraham. Isaac is afraid and says that Rebekah is his sister. Then Abimelech looks out of a window and sees Isaac caressing his wife. He commands that no one touch Isaac or his wife.

Isaac sows and reaps a hundred times what he planted in a single year. The envious Philistines fill in the wells Abraham’s servants dug, and Abimelech sends him away. Isaac digs the wells again, and two new ones bring quarrels. The third brings none, and he says, “For now the LORD has made room for us,” before going up to Beersheba, where the LORD appears again, and Abimelech comes to make a covenant. “We saw plainly that the LORD was with you.” The chapter ends with Esau’s Hittite wives, who grieve his parents.

Isaac’s story echoes Abraham’s: a famine, a king named Abimelech, a wife called a sister and a dispute over wells at Beersheba (see Genesis 12, 20 and 21). The chapter shows a quieter patriarch, who answers a conflict by moving on. The covenant promise is passed on to him “for my servant Abraham’s sake.”

Isaac is old and cannot see. He calls Esau, his elder son, and asks him to hunt and make savory food, so that he may bless him before he dies. Rebekah overhears. She calls Jacob, tells him what to do and says that any curse will be on her. She dresses Jacob in Esau’s clothes and puts goatskins on his hands and neck.

Jacob goes to his father. Isaac is unsure: “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” He asks again and then blesses Jacob. Esau comes in with his own food, and Isaac trembles violently. Esau cries out, “Bless me, even me also, my father.” There is one more blessing, but it speaks of a sword and a yoke. Esau hates Jacob and says in his heart that he will kill him once their father is dead. Rebekah hears, and sends Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran.

The chapter tells of a family torn by favorites and by deceit, and the narrator does not hold Jacob up as an example. Later chapters show what the deceit costs him: Jacob, who deceives his father, is himself deceived by Laban in Genesis 29. The blessing on Esau looks ahead to Edom, which is Esau’s line (Genesis 36). Isaac’s words also show how much a spoken blessing could mean.

Isaac blesses Jacob and sends him to Paddan Aram, to the family of Laban. Jacob leaves Beersheba toward Haran.

Night falls, and he stops where he is. He takes one of the stones of the place for a pillow and lies down. He dreams: a stairway is set on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God are going up and down on it. The LORD stands above it. He is the God of Abraham and Isaac, and the land under Jacob will be his. His offspring will be like the dust of the earth, and all the families of the earth will be blessed. “I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go,” and he will bring Jacob back.

Jacob wakes. “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I didn’t know it.” He sets up the stone as a pillar, names the place Bethel. Then he makes a vow.

Jacob is a fugitive from his brother’s anger, and this is the first time in Genesis that God speaks to him. The stairway has been pictured in art for centuries; the Gospel of John echoes it in John 1. The promise given to Abraham is now repeated to Jacob. The vow to give a tenth is one of the earliest mentions of tithing in the Bible.

Jacob comes to a well in a field. The stone on its mouth is large. The shepherds know Laban, and just then his daughter Rachel arrives with the sheep. Jacob rolls the stone away alone and waters her flock. He kisses Rachel and weeps. Laban runs out and embraces him. “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.”

Jacob offers seven years of work for Rachel, and the years “seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her.” At the wedding feast Laban brings Leah in the evening. In the morning Jacob sees who it is and says, “Why then have you deceived me?” Laban answers that the younger cannot come before the elder, and Jacob agrees to seven more years.

The LORD sees that Leah is hated, and she bears four sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah. At the last she says, “This time I will praise the LORD.”

Jacob the deceiver now meets a deceiver in his own family. The chapter shows the pain of a house with two wives, and many readers note how much longing runs through Leah’s naming of her sons. Judah, the fourth, becomes the ancestor of David and, in Christian reading, of Jesus; see Matthew 1. Levi’s line later serves as the priests.

Rachel has no children, and she envies her sister. “Give me children, or else I will die.” Jacob’s anger burns: is he in God’s place? Rachel gives him her servant Bilhah, and Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah, who has stopped bearing, gives her servant Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Over mandrakes, Leah and Rachel bargain for a night with Jacob, and Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun and a daughter, Dinah.

Then God remembers Rachel and opens her womb. She bears Joseph and says, “God has taken away my reproach.”

Jacob asks Laban to let him go home, but Laban begs him to stay, since the LORD has blessed him for Jacob’s sake. They agree on wages of the speckled and spotted animals. Laban moves his own flock away, while Jacob peels rods and sets them before the flocks in the watering troughs. The stronger animals become his. He grows exceedingly rich.

The chapter lists the births of most of the twelve tribes of Israel. Servants are given as wives in a rivalry between two sisters, and the text reports it without comment; many readers see the grief behind it. The wage deal and the peeled rods are told in detail. Jacob himself later credits God for the flocks (Genesis 31:9).

Laban’s sons grumble about Jacob, and Jacob sees Laban’s face: it is not toward him as before. The LORD says, “Return to the land of your fathers,” and Jacob calls Rachel and Leah to the field and tells them how Laban has changed his wages ten times, and how God has not let it hurt him. The sisters answer, “whatever God has said to you, do.”

They leave while Laban is away, and Rachel steals her father’s household gods. After three days Laban hears, and he pursues for seven days until God warns him in a dream not to speak to Jacob either good or bad. He asks why Jacob fled, and why his gods were stolen. Laban searches every tent, but Rachel is sitting on them.

Jacob’s anger spills out over twenty years of work. They make a covenant and raise a heap of stones: “The LORD watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another.”

The words of the heap are sometimes used today as a blessing between friends, but in this chapter they are a boundary pact between two men who do not trust each other. The household gods were small images; some scholars link them with a claim to inheritance. Jacob has now been away for twenty years. The chapter ends with Laban kissing his daughters, and he goes home.

Jacob is going home, and the angels of God meet him on the way. “This is God’s army.” He sends messengers ahead, and they return with the news that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob is greatly afraid. He divides his people into two companies and prays to be delivered from Esau, reminding God of his promise. He sends gifts ahead.

In the night he sends his family over the ford of the Jabbok, and stays alone. A man wrestles with him until daybreak. When the man sees he cannot win, he touches Jacob’s thigh and it is strained. “Let me go, for the day breaks.” Jacob says, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me.” The man asks his name and gives him a new one: Israel. Jacob names the place Peniel, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.” The sun rises on him, and he limps.

The man at the Jabbok is not named. Jacob says he has seen God, and Hosea 12 looks back on the scene. Jewish and Christian readers have taken the figure in more than one way, some as an angel, some as God appearing in human form. The new name Israel becomes the name of the whole people. The sinew at the hip gives a reason for a food custom, which the text says continues to this day.

Jacob looks up and sees Esau coming with four hundred men. He arranges his family, with the servants and their children first, Leah and hers next, and Rachel and Joseph last. Then he walks out in front and bows to the ground seven times.

Esau runs to meet him, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, and they weep. Esau asks who the women and children are, and one by one they come and bow. Esau asks about the company he met on the road, and Jacob says it was to find favor. Esau says, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.” Jacob presses the gift on him: “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.” Esau accepts.

Esau goes back to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth, then to Shechem, buys a parcel of land and builds an altar.

After the fear of chapter 32 comes the meeting no one expected. The text does not say they met again until they buried their father together; see Genesis 35. The ground Jacob buys at Shechem is important later in Israel’s story, and it is the setting of the next chapter. Many readers hear in this scene a picture of forgiveness between brothers.

Dinah, Leah’s daughter, goes out to see the daughters of the land. Shechem, the son of Hamor, the prince of the land, sees her. He takes her, lies with her and humbles her. Then he loves her, and asks his father to get her as his wife.

Hamor and Shechem offer marriages between the peoples and a generous dowry. Jacob’s sons answer with deceit. They will agree only if every male is circumcised. The men of the city consent. On the third day, while the men are sore, Simeon and Levi take swords, come upon the unsuspecting city and kill all the males. They bring Dinah out, and the other sons plunder the city. Jacob says they have made him odious to the land. They reply, “Should he deal with our sister as with a prostitute?”

This is one of the most painful chapters in Genesis. Dinah never speaks in it, and most readers understand verse 2 as describing sexual violence against her. The sons answer wrong with a worse wrong, and they turn the sign of the covenant into a trap. Jacob will remember what Simeon and Levi did at the end of his life (Genesis 49:5 to 7). The text gives no one in this story a clean victory.

God tells Jacob to go up to Bethel and to build an altar there. Jacob says to his household, “Put away the foreign gods that are among you,” and to purify themselves and change their garments. They hand over the gods, and Jacob hides them under the oak at Shechem. A terror of God keeps the cities around from pursuing them.

At Bethel he builds the altar. God appears again, blesses him, and says that his name is Israel. Jacob sets up a pillar and pours oil on it.

Then, on the road to Ephrath, Rachel goes into hard labor. The midwife says, “Don’t be afraid, for now you will have another son.” As her soul departs she names the boy Benoni, but his father calls him Benjamin. Rachel is buried on the way to Bethlehem. Reuben lies with Bilhah, and the twelve sons are listed. Isaac dies at one hundred eighty, and Esau and Jacob bury him.

Jacob returns to the place of his vow in Genesis 28. The promises there are renewed, now to a man whose name has changed. Rachel’s tomb near Bethlehem is remembered in the prophets; see Jeremiah 31 and Matthew 2. The list of the twelve sons gathers in one place the names of the tribes of Israel.

Esau has a story too, and the chapter tells it as a family record. Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan, and also a daughter of Ishmael. He took his wives, his sons and daughters, all his household and animals, and went to a land away from his brother Jacob. Their possessions were too great for them to live together. “Esau is Edom.” He lived in the hill country of Seir.

Then the names come: his sons, his grandsons and the chiefs who came from them. The Horites, who lived in Seir before, are listed too. One small detail stands out: Anah found hot springs in the wilderness while feeding his father’s donkeys. The chapter ends with the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel, and a list of Edom’s chiefs by their places.

A chapter of names can feel like a locked door, but it matters in the story. The older brother does not disappear. He becomes a nation, as the oracle in Genesis 25 said. Edom is later a neighbor and rival of Israel; see Numbers 20 and Obadiah. Amalek, who appears in verse 12, becomes an enemy in Exodus 17.

Joseph is seventeen, feeding the flock with his brothers, and he brings his father a bad report about them. Israel loves Joseph more than all his sons, because he was born in his old age, and gives him a tunic of many colors. His brothers see it and hate him. Then Joseph tells them his dreams. In one, their sheaves bow down to his; in another, the sun, moon and eleven stars do. Even his father rebukes him, though he keeps the saying in mind.

His father sends him to check on his brothers in Shechem, and then to Dothan. They see him far off. “Behold, this dreamer comes.” They plan to kill him. Reuben speaks against it, and they throw him into an empty pit. Judah suggests selling him, and merchants take him to Egypt. They dip the tunic in goat’s blood and bring it to their father. He tears his clothes, and “he refused to be comforted.”

Here begins the story of Joseph, which runs to the end of Genesis. The family that is chosen to bless the nations is cracked open by favoritism, envy and cruelty. Reuben and Judah each try to soften what happens. They will each appear again, in Genesis 42 to 44. Joseph is sold at the end of the chapter to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh.

Judah leaves his brothers, marries a Canaanite woman and has three sons. His firstborn, Er, marries Tamar, but Er is wicked in the LORD’s sight, and dies. Judah tells Onan to raise up offspring for Er. Onan knows the child won’t be his, and he refuses; that is evil in the LORD’s sight, and he dies too. Judah sends Tamar home to wait for his youngest son, Shelah, and then does not send for her.

Tamar sees that Shelah is grown and she has not been given to him. She covers her face with a veil and sits by the road. Judah takes her for a prostitute and leaves his signet, cord and staff. She conceives. Judah hears that Tamar is pregnant, and says, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.” She sends the pledge: whose are these? Judah says, “She is more righteous than I,” and knows her no more. Twins are born, Perez and Zerah.

The story interrupts Joseph’s, and it turns on a man who is made to see himself. The duty Judah names is described in Deuteronomy 25, and it was meant to protect a widow and her husband’s name. Tamar and Perez appear in the line of Jesus in Matthew 1. Judah is the same man who will later offer himself for Benjamin in Genesis 44.

Joseph is brought down to Egypt and bought by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. “The LORD was with Joseph,” and everything he touches prospers, and Potiphar sees it. Joseph is made overseer.

Then his master’s wife sets her eyes on him. “Lie with me.” He refuses. “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Day after day he does not listen. One day, with no one else inside, she catches him by his garment. He leaves it in her hand and runs outside.

She calls out to the men of her house and says the Hebrew came in to mock her. She keeps his garment until her husband comes home, and tells him the same story. Potiphar’s wrath is kindled, and he puts Joseph in the prison where the king’s prisoners are held. But the LORD is with him there too. The keeper of the prison puts all the prisoners in his hand.

A garment taken from Joseph has become evidence against him once more; the tunic in Genesis 37 was the first. The woman calls him the Hebrew, and the text shows how a foreigner and a servant could be treated when it was one word against another. The chapter shows Joseph wronged twice, yet repeats that the LORD was with him. It does not say how long he stays in prison.

Pharaoh’s chief cup bearer and chief baker have offended the king, and they are sent to the prison where Joseph is. He is assigned to care for them. Joseph finds them sad one morning. Each has dreamed in the same night, and no one can interpret it. “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” Joseph says. “Please tell it to me.”

The cup bearer dreams of a vine with three branches and grapes pressed into Pharaoh’s cup. Joseph says that in three days Pharaoh will restore him. One plea: “remember me when it is well with you.” He was stolen away from the land of the Hebrews and has done nothing to deserve the dungeon. The baker dreams of three baskets on his head, with birds eating from the top one. Joseph must tell him that in three days Pharaoh will hang him on a tree. On Pharaoh’s birthday it happens. “Yet the chief cup bearer didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him.”

The chapter turns on two dreams and a forgotten request. Many scholars note that dream interpretation was a recognized skill across the ancient Near East, but Joseph gives the credit to God, as he will again before Pharaoh. The story also makes the reader wait, because Joseph stays in prison; the next chapter begins two years later.

Two years pass, and Pharaoh dreams. Seven fat cattle come up from the river and are eaten by seven thin ones. Seven good heads of grain are swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. His spirit is troubled, and none of Egypt’s magicians can explain it. Then the cup bearer remembers a young Hebrew in prison.

Joseph is brought out. Pharaoh says he can interpret dreams, and Joseph answers, “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” The dream is one: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Joseph advises storing grain and finding a wise man to lead. Pharaoh asks, “a man in whom is the Spirit of God?” and sets Joseph over Egypt, with his signet ring.

In the good years he stores grain without number. He names his second son Ephraim: “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” When famine comes, all countries come to Egypt to buy grain.

From a dungeon to second place in the land in one day: the story turns on God being named in front of a king. Egypt takes seriously the work of storing food in good years, and the plan is Joseph’s. His sons’ names, Manasseh and Ephraim, mark his past and present, and Jacob blesses both in Genesis 48. The famine sets up the journey of his brothers.

The famine has reached Canaan, and Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt to buy grain. He keeps Benjamin at home. When they reach the man in charge, they bow with their faces to the ground. Joseph recognizes them, but they do not recognize him. He remembers his dreams and speaks roughly: “You are spies!”

They explain that they are twelve brothers, one is no more, and the youngest is with their father. After three days in custody he lets them go, all but one, until they bring the youngest. Alone together, they say, “We are certainly guilty concerning our brother,” remembering his begging. Reuben says he warned them. Joseph, listening through an interpreter, turns away and weeps. He keeps Simeon, binds him before their eyes, and fills their sacks with grain, putting each man’s money back.

On the way home, one opens his sack. “What is this that God has done to us?” Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go.

The dreams of Genesis 37 come true in front of Joseph, though no one at the table knows it. The text does not say what he intends, and readers differ: some see a test, some see a man holding back his feelings. Notice that the brothers now speak of guilt for the first time. Reuben offers his two sons as a pledge, and Jacob will not listen.

The famine is severe, and the grain is gone. Jacob tells his sons to go down again. Judah speaks: the man warned them not to return without their brother. “I’ll be collateral for him.” If he does not bring Benjamin back, he will bear the blame forever. He tells them to take choice fruits of the land, balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts and almonds, and double money, and he prays that God Almighty will give them mercy.

In Egypt they are brought to Joseph’s house, and they are afraid. The steward says, “Peace be to you. Don’t be afraid.” He tells them their God has given them treasure in their sacks, and brings Simeon out. At noon Joseph comes and asks about their old father. He sees Benjamin and hurries out to weep. Then he washes his face and orders the meal. They are seated by age. Benjamin’s portion is five times as much as any of theirs.

Judah, who suggested selling Joseph in Genesis 37 and failed Tamar in Genesis 38, now steps forward and puts his own life behind his brother. The Egyptian steward speaks of the God of their father, which shows that the household knows something of Joseph’s faith. The chapter says that Egyptians did not eat with Hebrews, so the meal is set with three tables.

The brothers leave at dawn with full sacks. Joseph has told his steward to put his silver cup in the youngest brother’s sack. When they are not yet far from the city, the steward overtakes them. “Why have you rewarded evil for good?” They protest: whoever has it should die, and the rest will be slaves. The steward says only the one who has it will be a slave.

The sacks are opened from the oldest to the youngest. The cup is found in Benjamin’s. They tear their clothes and go back. At Joseph’s house Judah says, “God has found out the iniquity of your servants.”

Judah steps up and tells the whole story again: their father’s love for the boy, his own promise, the grief that would follow. He offers himself as a slave in the boy’s place: “For how will I go up to my father, if the boy isn’t with me?”

Joseph tests his brothers with the same situation that once led them to betray him: a favored son in danger, and a chance to walk away. The man who proposed the sale in Genesis 37 now offers himself as the slave. The steward’s words about divination are part of the story that Joseph tells, and the text does not praise the practice. Genesis 45 gives the answer.
